issues.legal_issue: A special statutory regime governing a temple’s endowments prevails over an inconsistent general enactment that purports to treat those endowments as trust estates and vest them elsewhere.
material_facts: The disputed lands were treated as properties of the temple and its endowments.
The temple-specific statute vested administration and governance of the temple and its endowments in its managing committee and empowered the committee to possess temple properties.
A later amendment to the general estate-abolition statute deemed estates belonging to the temple to be trust estates, and a notification purported to vest those estates in the State.
The lands had already been statutorily vested in the temple’s managing committee under the temple-specific regime.
issues.conclusion: The temple-specific statute prevailed. The part of the general statute’s proviso deeming the temple’s estates to be trust estates, and the related vesting notification insofar as they applied to the temple’s lands, were struck down or quashed; the disputed lands remained vested in the temple’s managing committee.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 5 and 30 of the Shri Jagannath Temple Act, 1955 provided for statutory vesting and government superintendence of the temple and its endowments; Section 33 concerned the committee’s possession of temple property. The first part of the proviso to Section 2(oo) and the notification under Section 3-A of the Orissa Estates Abolition Act, 1951 could not override that special regime. The Court applied the principle generalia specialibus non derogant and the rules of harmonious construction, relying on U.P. State Electricity Board v. Hari Shankar Jain, LIC v. D.J. Bahadur, Commercial Tax Officer v. Binani Cements Ltd., and J.K. Cotton Spinning and Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of U.P. It also relied on Raja Bira Kishore Deb v. State of Orissa regarding the temple statute and on Mahant Shri Srinivas Ramanuj Das v. Surjanarayan Das for the distinction between Math properties and temple properties.

predicates.temple_property_ownership_and_statutory_: The proceeding concerns ownership of temple property and a conflict between statutory regimes governing that property.
predicates.property_is_an_endowment_of_a_temple: The property at issue is an endowment belonging to a temple.
predicates.special_law_statutorily_vests_temple_end: A law specifically governing the temple vests its endowments in a designated temple body.
predicates.later_general_law_conflicts_with_that_ve: A general law later purports to classify or vest the same property in a way inconsistent with the special-law vesting.

issues.definition: When a temple-property ownership proceeding involves an endowment already vested under a temple-specific law and a conflicting general-law treatment, the special-law vesting prevails.

issues.legal_issue: A prior judgment does not bar a later challenge to a different order on res judicata grounds, and a prior decision made without considering controlling legislation does not bind the court on that omitted issue.
material_facts: The earlier proceeding concerned the validity of a notification vesting estates in the State.
The later proceeding challenged a subsequent settlement order and raised the effect of the temple-specific statute on the property.
The earlier judgment considered the general estate-abolition statute but did not consider the temple-specific statute or the relevant law on priority between special and general enactments.
issues.conclusion: Res judicata did not bar the later proceeding because the subject matter was not identical. The earlier judgment was per incuriam insofar as it upheld vesting without considering the temple-specific statute and the applicable law on conflicting enactments.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires, among other things, that the matter directly and substantially in issue in the later proceeding be the same as that finally decided in the earlier proceeding; the Court relied on Sheodan Singh v. Daryao Kunwar and Syed Mohd. Salie Labbai v. Mohd. Hanifa. A decision rendered in ignorance of an applicable statute or binding authority may be per incuriam; the Court relied on Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Gurnam Kaur, State of U.P. v. Synthetics and Chemicals Ltd., and Fuerst Day Lawson Ltd. v. Jindal Exports Ltd. It also noted the flexible character of stare decisis as discussed in State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat.

predicates.later_proceeding_challenges_a_different_: The later proceeding challenges an order different from the order considered in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.res_judicata_issue_arises: A party invokes the effect of an earlier final judgment to bar a later proceeding.
predicates.issues_in_two_proceedings_are_not_identi: The matter directly and substantially in issue in the later proceeding is not the same as the matter finally decided earlier.
predicates.prior_judgment_omitted_controlling_law: The earlier judgment did not consider legislation or binding law controlling the issue now raised.

issues.definition: When a later proceeding challenges a different order and either the issues are not identical or the earlier judgment omitted controlling law, the earlier judgment does not bar the later proceeding or control the omitted issue.

issues.legal_issue: A settlement claim under the estate-abolition regime cannot be sustained where the claimant has not established its basis as an intermediary and the settlement is decided by an official lacking authority to perform the required quasi-judicial function.
material_facts: The Math filed a claim for settlement of lands under the estate-abolition statute.

The claim form identified the land as in the claimant’s own possession but did not provide the requested details of a temporary lessee or mortgagee, leaving the basis of the claim as an intermediary unclear.
The statute required claims to be filed before the Collector.
A Tahsildar passed an order settling lands, although the relevant settlement determination was quasi-judicial and the Tahsildar’s function under the statute was administrative.
The disputed lands were already vested in the temple body under the temple-specific statute.
issues.conclusion: The Math’s claim to settlement as an intermediary was untenable on the record, and the Tahsildar was not competent to make the quasi-judicial settlement order. The settlement in favour of the Math could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: Section 8-A of the Orissa Estates Abolition Act, 1951 required claims under Sections 6, 7 and 8 to be filed before the Collector. The Court treated the determination as quasi-judicial and held that such a function could not be delegated merely by relying on an inclusive definition of Collector. It relied on Bharat Bihari Mishra v. State of Orissa regarding the quasi-judicial nature of the proceeding and Basanti Kumar Sahu v. State of Orissa regarding the Tahsildar’s administrative role. The Court also held that the lands were already vested under the special temple statute and did not require settlement under the general statute.

predicates.statutory_land_settlement_claim: A claimant seeks settlement of land through a statutory process for claims by intermediaries.
predicates.claimant_has_not_shown_intermediary_basi: The claim record does not establish the facts on which the claimant asserts intermediary status.
predicates.settlement_requires_quasi_judicial_deter: The governing process requires a quasi-judicial decision on the settlement claim.
predicates.settlement_is_decided_by_official_withou: An official who lacks authority to perform the required quasi-judicial function makes the settlement decision.

issues.definition: A statutory land settlement order is invalid where the claimant has not shown an intermediary basis and an official without authority makes a determination that must be quasi-judicial.

issues.legal_issue: The invalidation of a statutory deeming provision and related vesting notification does not unsettle claims already settled under the estate-abolition regime.
material_facts: The Court struck down the part of the statutory proviso that deemed the temple’s estates to be trust estates and quashed the related vesting notification insofar as they covered the temple’s lands.
The Court expressly limited the effect of that ruling so that claims already settled under the estate-abolition statute would remain unaffected.
issues.conclusion: The striking down and quashing operated prospectively and did not affect claims already settled under the estate-abolition statute.
issues.legal_principle: The Court invoked Article 142 of the Constitution in shaping relief and expressly preserved claims already settled under the Orissa Estates Abolition Act, 1951 from the effect of its ruling.

predicates.statutory_validity_proceeding: The proceeding asks the court to rule on the validity or effect of a statutory measure governing property.
predicates.court_invalidates_a_general_property_ves: The court invalidates a general statutory measure that purported to classify or vest property.
predicates.claims_were_already_settled_under_that_r: Claims concerning the property had already been settled under the statutory regime before the court’s ruling.

issues.definition: When a court invalidates a general property-vesting measure but claims had already been settled under that regime, those settled claims remain unaffected.
